NRR: This fund simply holds NEAR, the token of the NEAR blockchain network, and stakes part of it to earn extra tokens as rewards. Its value is the price of one cryptocurrency, nothing else, so it carries the full boom and bust swings of crypto.
JULZ: Options on the S&P 500 built to take part of a market drop for you over an outcome period that refreshes each July, while surrendering some gains. It is aimed at nervous stock investors, and what you receive hinges on when in the period you buy.
PSFO: Options on the S&P 500 in a flexible outcome design, meant to join in market gains while keeping a measure of protection against losses, over a period ending each October. Flexibility means the protection level can vary, unlike the fixed promises of plain buffer funds.
STEN: It holds a big US stock fund and adds options targeting protection against roughly the first 10% of losses over a year starting each September, as the name says. In return, gains are capped, and the buffer only fully applies to those who hold the whole period.
QIDX: Companies of many sizes chosen for steady, growing earnings, led by technology, industrial and health care firms. The quality earnings focus aims for a dependable core holding, favoring businesses whose profits are consistent over flashy growers with uneven results.
FDIQ: The companies that run the plumbing of finance: stock exchanges, credit rating agencies, index makers and market data providers. They earn from trading and data fees rather than lending, so this is a focused bet on the business of financial information itself.
PBMY: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in May, matching the Buffer 20 in its name. The deep cushion is the draw, paid for with a cap on gains during strong market years.
XOMO: A single-stock income fund built on Exxon Mobil: it uses options to mimic owning the shares while selling covered calls for monthly income. The call selling caps how much it gains if the stock jumps, so it is an income play on one oil giant.
GLDB: A blend of bitcoin and gold, adjusted dynamically as a model weighs risk signals like volatility and momentum, with small side positions in silver and ethereum. It is pitched as an alternative to paper money, and its mix shifts as the model's signals change.
SEPT: Options on big US stocks that absorb the first 10% of a market loss over a year starting in September, exactly what the Buffer10 in the name promises. Gains above that are capped, so it is a cautious way to stay invested.
PBDE: Options on the S&P 500 set to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in December, the deep protection its Buffer 20 name describes. Investors give up part of any rally in exchange, making it a defensive, low-drama holding.
THEQ: Large US stocks picked through the manager's own research, held mainly through a house stock fund, with a derivatives hedge layered on top. The hedge reduces volatility and offers protection in downturns, aiming for stock exposure with smaller bumps along the way.
KSEP: Options on a small company index fund that cushion part of any loss over a year-long outcome period resetting each September. The cushion costs upside, since gains are capped, and the options make it steadier but less responsive than owning small company stocks outright.
OAKG: Large companies worldwide bought at prices Oakmark's managers consider below their true worth, spread across banks, health care, technology and consumer firms. It is a patient value portfolio of a few dozen picks, and the mix of US and foreign stocks changes as bargains shift.
TPFG: Fifty large and mid-sized growth companies picked for strong and rising free cash flow, drawn from a biblically screened universe. Technology and industrial firms dominate, and the Christian values screen sets it apart from typical growth funds.
SQLV: Hundreds of small US companies picked by a quantitative model looking for quality and value together: profitable firms at reasonable prices. The wide spread keeps any single company tiny, and the model trades often, so the lineup changes more than in most index funds.
AGGS: A disciplined core bond portfolio of US dollar debt: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and company bonds, chosen within strict risk limits. It aims to be a portfolio's steady anchor, with the managers adjusting the mix as rates and credit conditions change.
MAXI: It aims for bitcoin exposure that can range from about half to twice the fund's size, held through bitcoin funds and options, alongside an income strategy. That variable leverage makes it far wilder than simply holding bitcoin, closer to a trading tool than an investment.
HFND: It builds long and short positions across dozens of stock and bond funds and futures, trying to copy the returns of hedge fund multi-strategy portfolios. Because it goes both long and short, it aims to depend less on whether markets rise or fall.
LDDR: US Treasury bonds and government money market funds, arranged as an income bucket meant to pay out steady monthly income through 2035. Backed entirely by government debt, it trades growth for predictability, like a self-built pension with a fixed end year.
MUSE: Credit of many kinds from around the world: high yield bonds, bank loans and foreign debt including emerging markets, mixed actively by TCW. Spreading across credit sectors hunts for income wherever it looks best paid, with more risk than a plain corporate bond fund.
WCME: Companies in developing countries picked actively for quality growth, dominated by Asian chip makers plus banks and drug firms. WCM's concentrated, research-driven style means it looks quite different from a broad emerging markets index, for better or worse.
JULP: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb about the first eighth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in July, matching the Buffer 12 name. The moderate cushion leaves more upside than deeper buffers, but gains are still capped.
RAAA: The safest top slice of CLOs, the AAA-rated layers of bundled corporate loans, with borrowed money added to enhance the yield. AAA layers have historically been well protected, but the leverage and the complexity of loan bundles add risks ordinary bond funds do not have.
BRCE: Large US companies across every industry, chosen by blending old-fashioned analyst research with computer models, MFS's signature approach. It is built as a core stock holding, technology-heavy like today's market, with stock picking meant to add an edge over a plain index.
SLDR: US Treasury bonds arranged in a ladder, with pieces coming due steadily over the next one to three years. The ladder keeps income rolling in and money regularly freeing up, a conservative parking place that barely flinches when interest rates move.
AADR: Foreign companies traded in the US as ADRs, chosen by Dorsey Wright's momentum method, which favors stocks already rising. The lineup spans banks, drug makers, miners and tech from many countries, and it shifts toward whichever overseas markets are strongest.
IBTR: US Treasury bonds that come due around the end of 2036, when this fund itself ends and returns its money. Long-dated government debt like this pays income with no credit risk, but its price swings widely as long-term interest rates move.
VGVT: US government bonds and government-backed mortgage bonds of all maturities, actively managed by Vanguard's bond team. It aims to be a safe, steady core bond holding, with the managers shifting maturities as they judge where rates are heading.
FTBD: A go-anywhere bond fund that roams the whole debt market, from Treasuries to high yield and emerging market bonds, in dollars and hedged foreign currencies. The tactical freedom lets Fidelity chase income wherever it appears, so the risk level varies over time.
CPST: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to protect against losses over an outcome period that resets each September, with participation in gains limited in exchange. It offers big-company stock exposure with a safety net, designed to be held for the full period.
TXXI: A blend of municipal bonds and taxable bonds of medium length, mixed to maximize what an investor keeps after taxes. At least half sits in tax-free municipals, with taxable bonds added when they pay better even after tax, a balancing act few funds attempt.
FLGR: Germany's large and mid-sized companies: industrial and engineering giants, big insurers and banks, and its software leaders. It is a single-country bet on Europe's biggest economy, moving with German exports, the euro and European politics.
DURA: Companies paying high dividends that also pass tests for financial strength and reasonable prices, spread across health care, energy, everyday goods and utilities. The durability screen aims for income that survives downturns, not just the biggest yields on offer.
GHTA: A tactical mix of other funds, currently leaning on bonds and floating rate Treasuries with a smaller stock slice, shifted by the managers' risk models. It can change posture a lot, from cautious to aggressive, depending on how dangerous the managers judge markets to be.
HEMI: US stocks chosen by Wellington researchers for improving quality and momentum, paired with option selling that harvests extra premium income. The premiums add a steady payout on top of dividends, in exchange for giving up part of the stocks' biggest gains.
NOVZ: Options on the S&P 500 meant to absorb part of a market decline over an outcome period that restarts each November, while keeping a share of the gains. Actively managed, it trades some upside for peace of mind, and timing your purchase affects the result.
GYLD: One hundred fifty of the highest yielding investments worldwide, gathered across property companies, energy partnerships, dividend stocks and bonds. Chasing the world's biggest yields pays high income, but high yield usually signals high risk somewhere, so holdings can be shaky.
HYP: Fast-growing companies picked actively across technology, energy and health care, hunting for businesses expanding at hypergrowth speed. These are mostly smaller, less proven names, so the fund aims high and swings hard, a speculation rather than a core holding.
PBAP: Options on big US stocks built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in April, as its Buffer 20 name states. It favors protection over growth, so expect it to sit out much of any strong rally.
JANM: Options on the S&P 500 seeking the maximum loss buffer the market offers over a year starting in January, per the Max Buffer name. Protection that deep leaves only a thin slice of gains, so it is built for capital preservation, not growth.
FTDS: Companies with strong balance sheets and a record of raising their dividends year after year, led by banks, energy and industrial firms. The strength tests aim for dividends that keep growing through downturns, suiting investors who want income with staying power.
DECZ: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to soften part of a market drop over an outcome period that restarts each December, trading some upside for the cushion. It is one of a monthly series, so buyers can pick the starting month that suits their timing.
KCOP: Exposure to copper through mining companies, copper funds and derivatives, with option selling layered on to add income. Copper prices ride global construction and electrification demand, so the fund swings with the industrial cycle, while the options work pays extra along the way.
VUSG: Large and mid-sized US growth companies picked actively by Wellington, the firm behind Vanguard's oldest fund, with technology over half the portfolio. It aims to beat plain growth indexes through stock picking, so it can pull ahead or fall behind its benchmarks for stretches.
AZTD: Small and mid-sized companies from developed markets across North America, Europe and the Pacific, picked by stock selection models. Smaller foreign firms get less attention from big investors, which is the opportunity, and currency moves add another layer of ups and downs.
FXED: Income investments of many stripes: corporate bonds, preferred shares, lending companies and bond funds, blended to enhance the payout. Reaching across riskier corners of the bond world lifts the income, with correspondingly more credit risk than a plain investment grade fund.
PBNV: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in November, the promise in its Buffer 20 name. Deep protection like this means muted gains, suiting investors who fear losses more than missing rallies.
TGLR: High quality large companies chosen for strong earnings and dividend growth plus an above-average dividend yield, spread across technology, banks and industry. It blends value discipline with growth in payouts, a new era take on classic dividend value investing.
TMLP: Master limited partnerships that move, process and store oil and gas, held through swaps rather than directly to sidestep the tax headaches MLPs create for funds. These pipeline partnerships pay generous distributions, and their prices follow energy volumes and oil markets.
